newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - LVMH cuts Guinness stake.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - LVMH cuts Guinness stake.

text.p: French luxury goods group LVMH said on Friday it had sold a third of its 21 percent stake in British drinks group Guinness Plc to help pay for the acquisition of U.S. duty free chain DFS.

"LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton has sold 135,081,327 shares of Guinness Plc, equivalent to approximately seven percent of the total number of shares outstanding, to Goldman Sachs, thereby reducing its stake to approximately 14 percent," LVMH said in a statement.
U.S. broker Goldman Sachs was placing the shares at around 414 pence in the market, dealers said, putting the total value of the sale at 559 million sterling ($934.7 million), or 5.05 billion francs.
LVMH said it would keep the 14 percent stake in Guinness and seek to develop the longstanding business ties between the two companies, which formed an alliance more than 10 years ago.

An LVMH spokeswoman said the decision to sell part of the Guinness stake reflected a shift in LVMH's horizon following its 12.9 billion franc purchase of control of U.S. duty free chain DFS earlier this month.

Speculation had been rife that LVMH might trim its Guinness stake after taking on such a large acquisition even though it had the means to finance the DFS deal. Before the deal, it had three billion francs of debt and equity of 35 billion.
"The sale of part of the Guinness stake will serve to finance a portion of the DFS acquisition," the spokeswoman said.
Shares in LVMH surged 3.7 percent to 1,558 francs in mid-morning trade on the Paris bourse.
LVMH and Guinness have held cross-shareholdings since the late 1980s, but the relationship weakened as the profitability of the drinks business declined relative to luxury goods.
In 1994 the two companies restructured their cross-holdings leaving LVMH with 21 percent of Guinness, which in turn held 34 percent of Moet Hennessy, LVMH's champagne and cognac business.
LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault began putting pressure on Guinness last year to increase shareholder value.
A French luxury goods analyst said the decision to sell some Guinness shares now may have been prompted by sterling's recent rise against the franc.
